title: Logs and traces: ELK, EFK and OpenTelemetry
intro: Parts 9 and 10 told you when hello-devops is unhealthy. This part gives you the two signals that say which request failed and where its time went. Days 47 and 48 collect every log line into Elasticsearch with Fluent Bit, first with Docker Compose on your laptop and then as a DaemonSet on kind. Day 49 traces hello-devops with OpenTelemetry, without changing its code, and finds a slow Redis call in Jaeger.

lessons.title: Centralized logging and the Elastic stack
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain why teams centralize logs, run Elasticsearch, Kibana and Fluent Bit on your laptop, and find hello-devops errors in Kibana with KQL and ES|QL.

guess.q: A log line says `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError: Error -2 connecting to redis:6379`. You search Elasticsearch for `ConnectionError` and get zero hits. Why?
options: New logs need a few minutes before Elasticsearch can search them
Elasticsearch stored `redis.exceptions.connectionerror` as one word, and search matches whole words
Search is case-sensitive, so you have to type `connectionerror` in lower case
Elasticsearch only searches the first 256 characters of each log line
guess.why: Elasticsearch splits text into words (tokens) and searches those, not substrings. Dots between letters do not split a word, so the whole dotted name became one token, and `ConnectionError` on its own is not in the index.

terms.plain: Copying the logs of every app and server to one place where you can search them together.
A log line written as data with named fields, usually one JSON object per line.
One JSON object stored in Elasticsearch. In logging, one document is usually one log event.
A named collection of documents, such as hello-logs-2026.10.30, that you write to and search.
A table from each word to the documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book.
The list of fields in an index and the type of each one, such as text, keyword, long or date.
A shard is one slice of an index. A replica is a copy of a shard kept on a different node.
A small open-source program that collects logs, parses them into fields and sends them on.

sections.h: Why logs need one home
sections.body:
In Part 3 you read a container's output with `docker logs`. That works for one app on one laptop. Now picture hello-devops on Kubernetes: three pods on three nodes, replaced on every deploy. A customer says a payment failed at 14:02. Which pod handled it? That pod may not exist any more, and its logs left with it.

Centralized logging fixes this. Every line every container prints is copied, as it is written, to one store you can search. The copy outlives the container, so you stop asking where the log is and start asking what it says.

Metrics from Part 9 tell you that errors went up. Logs tell you which request failed and why. You need both, and you usually read them in that order.

A log pipeline has four jobs. The lab gives each one to a different program:
1. The app prints one event per line to stdout. hello-devops already does.
2. A shipper collects the lines, parses them into fields and sends them on. Here that is Fluent Bit.
3. A store indexes every field so search is fast. Here that is Elasticsearch.
4. A web UI lets people search and chart. Here that is Kibana.

In the lab, Docker itself hands each line to Fluent Bit. The compose file sets the `fluentd` logging driver on the web container, so the Docker engine sends every line to port 24224 as well as keeping its own copy. One detail matters: the engine opens that connection, not a container. That is why the address is `localhost:24224`, the port Fluent Bit publishes on your laptop, and why `fluentd-async` is set. Without it, a container stops at once when it cannot reach its log collector.

sections.h: Write logs a machine can read
sections.body:
Compare two lines from the lab. Gunicorn prints this when it starts a worker:

`[2026-10-30 05:03:07 +0000] [8] [INFO] Booting worker with pid: 8`

And this is one line of the access log the lab turns on:

`{"level":"INFO","logger":"access","method":"GET","path":"/","status":200,"duration_ms":8}`

The first is fine for a human. A machine has to guess where the level ends and the message starts, and every program formats it a little differently. The second is a structured log: data with named fields. Fluent Bit turns each key into a field, so you can ask for `status >= 500` or the slowest `path` without writing a regular expression.

You did not change `app.py` to get this. The lab's compose file gives gunicorn an `--access-logformat` that prints JSON. In your own services, use a JSON logging library and write one event per line.

Every event also carries a level. Most teams use these four:
- DEBUG: detail for developers. Usually off in production, because it is loud.
- INFO: normal events, such as a request served or a job finished.
- WARN: something odd that has not failed yet, such as a retry.
- ERROR: a request or job failed, and someone may need to act.

Some things never belong in a log, because many people read the log store and it keeps data for weeks. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet says to remove, mask or hash these before they are written:
- passwords, access tokens and session IDs
- database connection strings and encryption keys
- payment card and bank account data
- personal data, such as names, email addresses and home addresses

A token in a log is a security incident. Deleting it later from every copy and backup is slow, painful work, so scrub at the source.

sections.h: Documents, indices and the inverted index
sections.body:
Elasticsearch stores JSON documents. A document is one JSON object, and in logging one document is one log event. Each document gets an `_id`, and Elasticsearch keeps the exact JSON you sent in a field called `_source`.

Documents live in an index, a named collection such as `hello-logs-2026.10.30`. You write to one index and can search many at once with a pattern like `hello-logs-*`. The lab makes one index per day, which keeps old days easy to delete.

Search is fast because of the **inverted index**. When a document arrives, Elasticsearch splits each text field into words, called tokens, and lowercases them. Then it records, for every token, which documents contain it. It works like the index at the back of a book: to find "declined" you look it up once instead of reading every page.

Here is what the default analyzer did with a message in the worked example:

`Payment FAILED for order 42: card declined` became `payment`, `failed`, `for`, `order`, `42`, `card` and `declined`.

That explains two surprises you will hit in the lab:
- A search for `payments` finds nothing. Only `payment` was stored, and the default analyzer does not reduce words to a common stem.
- `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError` stays one token, because dots between letters do not split words. Search for `ConnectionError` and you get zero hits. Search for the phrase `"service not known"` from the same error and you find it at once.

This trips most people up, because grep matches any substring and Elasticsearch matches whole tokens.

New documents are not searchable in the same instant. Elasticsearch makes them visible within about one second, in a step called a refresh. The Elastic docs call this near real-time search.

sections.h: Mappings: text, keyword and the first guess
sections.body:
Each index has a **mapping**: the type of every field and how it is indexed. You can write one yourself, or let Elasticsearch guess from the first document that contains a field. That guess is called dynamic mapping, and it sticks.

The two types you will meet most in logs are:
- `text`: split into tokens for full-text search. Good for `message` or `log`.
- `keyword`: stored whole, for exact filters, sorting and counting. Good for `level`, `path` or `service`.

A keyword is matched exactly, capitals included. In the worked example the `level` field held `ERROR`, so a search for `error` on it found nothing.

For strings, dynamic mapping makes both: a `text` field plus a `.keyword` sub-field. That is why the lab's index shows `path` and also `path.keyword`. Whole numbers become `long`, so `status` and `duration_ms` are numbers you can compare and average.

The guess is only as good as the first document:
- A service sends `"duration_ms": "120"` as a string. The field becomes text, and you can never average it in that index.
- A later document sends a value the mapped type cannot hold. Elasticsearch rejects it with a `document_parsing_exception` and HTTP status 400.
- Someone logs request headers as keys. Every new header becomes a new field. The Elastic docs warn that too many fields, a mapping explosion, can run the cluster out of memory.

The fix is an explicit mapping. On Day 48 you put one into an index template, so every new daily index starts with the right types.

sections.h: Shards, replicas and the yellow cluster
sections.body:
One running Elasticsearch process is a node. Nodes that work together form a cluster. Your lab is a cluster of one node.

An index is split into shards. Each shard is a complete small Lucene index (Lucene is the Java search library under Elasticsearch) holding part of the documents. Shards let one index spread over many nodes, so more machines can store and search it in parallel.

There are two kinds:
- A primary shard holds the original documents. Each document belongs to exactly one primary.
- A replica shard is a copy of a primary on another node. If that node dies, the copy takes over. Replicas also answer searches.

Two rules follow, and both surprise people:
1. The number of primary shards is fixed when the index is created. The number of replicas can change at any time.
2. Elasticsearch never puts a replica on the same node as its primary.

So on your laptop, an index with one replica is yellow: all data is there, but a copy is missing. Green means every shard is placed. Red means a primary is missing, so some data cannot be searched. The lab's daily index starts yellow for exactly this reason, because new indices get one replica by default. On Day 48 you set replicas to 0 for it.

More shards are not free. Each search runs on one thread per shard, and every shard costs memory. The Elastic sizing guide suggests shards between 10 GB and 50 GB. A lab that stores a few megabytes a day needs one shard per index.

sections.h: ELK, EFK and OpenSearch
sections.body:
ELK is the classic name for three Elastic products used together:
- Elasticsearch stores and searches.
- Logstash collects and reshapes data. It runs on the JVM and can do heavy transformations on the way in.
- Kibana is the web UI.

Elastic later added Beats, small single-purpose shippers such as Filebeat, and then Elastic Agent, one agent you manage centrally with Fleet. Elastic now calls the whole family the Elastic Stack.

EFK swaps the L for an F: Fluentd or Fluent Bit. Both are open-source CNCF graduated projects, not Elastic products. Fluentd came first and is written in C and Ruby. Fluent Bit is written in C for small machines. Its docs compare the two like this:
- Memory: Fluentd needs more than 60 MB, Fluent Bit about 450 KB.
- Plugins: Fluentd has over 1,000 external plugins, Fluent Bit over 100 built in.

You need neither Logstash nor Fluentd: Fluent Bit sends straight to Elasticsearch, as in the lab. On Kubernetes a shipper runs on every node, so a small footprint matters, and that is the job Fluent Bit was built for.

The licence history explains the other product name you will meet:
1. Until January 2021, Elasticsearch and Kibana were open source under Apache 2.0.
2. Elastic then switched to a choice of SSPL or the Elastic License, and neither counts as an open source licence. The stated aim was to stop cloud providers selling Elasticsearch as a service.
3. AWS forked the last Apache 2.0 code as OpenSearch. It is still Apache 2.0 and has been under the Linux Foundation since September 2024.
4. In August 2024 Elastic added AGPLv3 as a third option. It sits next to the other two, and the binaries did not change.

For you, two facts matter. The lab images are free to run. And OpenSearch is close enough to Elasticsearch that today's ideas carry over.

sections.h: Searching in Kibana: Discover, KQL and ES|QL
sections.body:
Kibana's Discover page is where you read logs. It has two query modes.

Classic mode needs a data view: a saved name pattern such as `hello-logs-*` plus the time field `@timestamp`. You type KQL, the Kibana Query Language, into the search bar. Each condition is a field, an operator and a value:
- `status >= 500` shows failed requests. It works because `status` is a number.
- `path: "/readyz" and not status: 200` combines two conditions.
- `log: "service not known"` finds a phrase inside a Python traceback.
- `not path: "/healthz"` hides the health checks Docker sends every 30 seconds.

ES|QL mode needs no data view. You write a pipeline, like a Unix pipe over your logs, where each step works on the rows from the step before. This query counts failed requests per path:

`FROM hello-logs-* | WHERE status >= 500 | STATS errors = COUNT(*) BY path | SORT errors DESC`

On the lab it returned 5 for `/readyz` and 3 for `/`. My rule of thumb: KQL to narrow down what you are looking at, ES|QL when the question needs counting, grouping or math. You can even mix them, because ES|QL accepts KQL inside `WHERE KQL("status >= 500")`.

Two habits save time:
- Check the time picker first. Discover shows the last 15 minutes by default, so older logs look missing.
- Add the fields you care about (`path`, `status`, `duration_ms`) as columns. Otherwise each row is one long summary.

steps.say: Start only Elasticsearch from the lab and ask who it is. A GET on the root returns the cluster name and version. `filter_path` trims the answer to the fields you name, which keeps output readable.

Create an index with an explicit mapping, so nothing is left to guessing: `level` and `service` are keywords, `message` is full text. Ask for 1 primary shard and 1 replica, on purpose, because step 6 needs the replica.

Store three log events. Elasticsearch picks each `_id`. Look at `_shards`: 2 copies were wanted (primary and replica) but only 1 was written, a first hint that the replica has nowhere to live. The last write asks for `refresh=true` so the next search sees all three at once.
steps.code:
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:9200/demo-logs/_doc -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"@timestamp":"2026-10-30T10:00:00Z","level":"ERROR","service":"checkout","message":"Payment FAILED for order 42: card declined"}'
{"_index":"demo-logs","_id":"MSBHi6EBJ7eB7uT9Rb6E","_version":1,"result":"created","_shards":{"total":2,"successful":1,"failed":0},"_seq_no":0,"_primary_term":1}
$ curl -s -X POST localhost:9200/demo-logs/_doc -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"@timestamp":"2026-10-30T10:00:05Z","level":"INFO","service":"checkout","message":"Payment accepted for order 43"}' > /dev/null

steps.say: Look inside the inverted index. `_analyze` shows the tokens a field would store. The text field splits and lowercases. The keyword field keeps the value whole, capitals and all.

Now search, and predict each answer before you read it. `payment` finds both payment events. `payments` finds nothing, because that token was never stored. A `term` query for `error` on the keyword field also finds nothing: the stored value is `ERROR`.

Find the missing copy. `_cat/shards` lists the primary (`p`) as STARTED and the replica (`r`) as UNASSIGNED, so the index is yellow. Replicas are a setting you can change on a live index, so set them to 0 and it turns green.

code.title: logging/compose.yaml
code.src:
# Centralized logging lab (Day 47): hello-devops -> Fluent Bit -> Elasticsearch -> Kibana.
#
# LOCAL LEARNING ONLY. Security is switched off, so anything that can reach
# port 9200 can read and delete every log. Never run this on a server.
#
# Start (from this logging/ folder):  docker compose up -d --build
# Kibana:                             http://localhost:5601
# Elasticsearch:                      http://localhost:9200
# Stop and delete the stored logs:    docker compose down -v
#
# Memory: give Docker Desktop at least 6 GB (Settings > Resources). See README.md.

services:
  elasticsearch:
    image: elasticsearch:9.5.5 # Docker Hub official image, built by Elastic (see README.md)
    environment:
      discovery.type: single-node     # one node: do not look for other nodes to form a cluster
      xpack.security.enabled: "false" # no passwords and no TLS (lab only)
      ES_JAVA_OPTS: -Xms1g -Xmx1g     # Java heap: 1 GB, fixed
    ports:
      - "9200:9200"
    volumes:
      - es-data:/usr/share/elasticsearch/data
    mem_limit: 2g
    healthcheck:
      # Healthy once the cluster answers and is not red. Yellow is fine on one node.
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "curl -s localhost:9200/_cluster/health | grep -qv '\"status\":\"red\"'"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 30

  kibana:
    image: kibana:9.5.5 # must be the same version as Elasticsearch
    environment:
      ELASTICSEARCH_HOSTS: http://elasticsearch:9200
    ports:
      - "5601:5601"
    mem_limit: 2g # Kibana logs a warning below 2 GB
    depends_on:
      elasticsearch:
        condition: service_healthy

  fluent-bit:
    image: fluent/fluent-bit:5.1.5
    command: ["-c", "/fluent-bit/etc/fluent-bit.yaml"]
    volumes:
      - ./fluent-bit.yaml:/fluent-bit/etc/fluent-bit.yaml:ro
    ports:
      # The Docker engine itself (not a container) connects here to hand over
      # the web container's logs, so the port must be published on localhost.
      - "24224:24224"
    depends_on:
      elasticsearch:
        condition: service_healthy

  web:
    build: .. # the hello-devops Dockerfile, one folder up
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      APP_VERSION: "1.0.0"
    # Same gunicorn as the Dockerfile, plus an access log: one JSON line per request.
    # %(m)s method, %(U)s path, %(s)s status code, %(M)s duration in milliseconds.
    command:
      - gunicorn
      - --bind=0.0.0.0:8000
      - --workers=2
      - --no-control-socket
      - --access-logfile=-
      - '--access-logformat={"level":"INFO","logger":"access","method":"%(m)s","path":"%(U)s","status":%(s)s,"duration_ms":%(M)s}'
      - app:app
    logging:
      driver: fluentd
      options:
        fluentd-address: localhost:24224    # Fluent Bit's published port
        fluentd-async: "true"               # start even if Fluent Bit is not up yet
        fluentd-sub-second-precision: "true" # keep the order of lines inside one second
        tag: hello.{{.Name}}                # Fluent Bit routes on this tag
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      fluent-bit:
        condition: service_started

  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

volumes:
  es-data:

code.title: logging/fluent-bit.yaml
code.src:
# Fluent Bit pipeline for the logging lab (Days 47 and 48).
# Docker's fluentd logging driver sends each line the web container prints.
# Each record arrives with four fields: log (the line), source (stdout or stderr),
# container_id and container_name. The tag is hello.<container name>.

service:
  flush: 1        # send to outputs every second
  log_level: info

parsers:
  # Reads a JSON string and turns its keys into fields.
  - name: json_line
    format: json

multiline_parsers:
  # hello-devops prints two kinds of first lines: gunicorn and Flask messages
  # start with "[" (a timestamp) and access log lines start with "{".
  # Any other line (traceback frames, ^^^ markers, blank lines) belongs to
  # the event above it.
  - name: hello_multiline
    type: regex
    flush_timeout: 1000
    rules:
      - state: start_state
        regex: '/^[\[{]/'
        next_state: cont
      - state: cont
        regex: '/^(?![\[{])/'
        next_state: cont

pipeline:
  inputs:
    # Listen for the Docker logging driver (the Fluentd "forward" protocol).
    - name: forward
      listen: 0.0.0.0
      port: 24224

  filters:
    # 1. A Python traceback arrives as many lines. Glue them back into one record.
    #    (Fluent Bit's built-in "python" parser misses the ^^^ lines that
    #    Python 3.11 and later print, so we use our own rules above.)
    - name: multiline
      match: 'hello.*'
      multiline.key_content: log
      multiline.parser: hello_multiline

    # 2. If "log" holds JSON (the gunicorn access log), turn it into fields.
    #    Lines that are not JSON pass through unchanged.
    - name: parser
      match: 'hello.*'
      key_name: log
      parser: json_line
      reserve_data: on # keep the other fields (source, container_name, ...)

  outputs:
    - name: es
      match: 'hello.*'
      host: elasticsearch
      port: 9200
      logstash_format: on      # one index per day: hello-logs-YYYY.MM.DD, plus an @timestamp field
      logstash_prefix: hello-logs
      suppress_type_name: on   # required for Elasticsearch 8 and 9
      trace_error: on          # print Elasticsearch's answer when it rejects a record

    # Also print every record, so `docker compose logs fluent-bit` shows what leaves.
    - name: stdout
      match: '*'
      format: json_lines

lessons.mistake: Treating the Kibana search box like grep. You search for part of a word, such as `ConnectionError` inside `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError`, get zero hits, and decide the error never happened. Elasticsearch matches whole tokens. Search for a phrase that really appears as words (`"service not known"`), or filter on structured fields such as `status >= 500`. Check the tokens with `_analyze` before you trust an empty result.
lessons.real_world: On a payments team, every service writes JSON logs with the same field names (`service`, `level`, `order_id`, `trace_id`), so one Kibana query works across all of them. Card numbers and tokens are masked inside the app before the line is printed, and a review checks new log statements for personal data. When a merchant reports a failed payment, on-call filters on `order_id` and reads the whole story across services in a minute.

task.title: Find hello-devops errors in Kibana
steps: Give Docker Desktop at least 6 GB of memory (Settings, Resources). Add `logging/compose.yaml` and `logging/fluent-bit.yaml` from this lesson to your hello-devops repo.
Start the stack from the `logging` folder and wait until Elasticsearch is healthy.
Send 20 requests to http://localhost:8000/ and confirm that a `hello-logs-*` index exists and its document count grows.
Stop Redis, call `/` and `/readyz` a few times to create failures, then start Redis again.
Open Kibana at http://localhost:5601, create a data view for `hello-logs-*` with the time field `@timestamp`, and open Discover.
Use KQL to show only the failed requests, with `path`, `status` and `duration_ms` as columns.
Find the document that holds the Python traceback for one of the 500s and read which line of `app.py` failed.
Switch Discover to ES|QL and count failed requests per path. Keep the stack running if you go on to Day 48, or stop it with `docker compose down -v`.
hints: `status` is a number field, so comparison operators such as `>=` work on it.
The traceback is in the `log` field. Search for a phrase from the error message, not for one long dotted word.
If Discover is empty, widen the time picker before you suspect Fluent Bit.
task.done_when: You are done when Discover shows only the 500 and 503 requests and you have found the traceback line `File "/app/app.py", line 27, in count_visit`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate how a line that hello-devops prints ends up searchable in Kibana, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention the logging driver, Fluent Bit, the index and the inverted index.
explain_back.answer: The app prints each event as a line on stdout, and Docker's fluentd logging driver sends every line to Fluent Bit on port 24224. Fluent Bit glues tracebacks back together, turns JSON lines into fields and sends the records to Elasticsearch, which stores each one as a document in that day's hello-logs index. While storing it, Elasticsearch splits text fields into tokens and records which documents contain each token: the inverted index. Kibana's queries look tokens up in that table, which is why search is fast and why it matches whole words, not substrings.

recap: Centralized logging copies every line to one store, so logs outlive the containers that wrote them.
Structured JSON logs give you fields to filter on. Never log secrets or personal data.
Elasticsearch stores JSON documents in indices and finds them through an inverted index of tokens.
Mappings decide field types. Text is split into words, keyword is matched whole, and the first guess sticks.
Replicas never share a node with their primary, so a one-node lab with replicas is yellow.
ELK uses Logstash, EFK uses Fluentd or Fluent Bit, and OpenSearch is the Apache 2.0 fork.

check.q: Your logs get a new field, `customer_tier`, with values like `gold` and `silver`. You want to filter on it and count requests per tier. Which mapping type fits?
options: text
short
boolean
keyword
check.why: Exact filters and counts need the whole value stored as one term, which is what keyword does.

check.q: On your one-node lab you create an index with 2 primary shards and 2 replicas. What health do you expect for it?
options: Green, because one node can hold all shards
Yellow, because the replicas cannot share the node with their primaries
Red, because there are more shards than nodes
Green after one minute, once the replicas copy over
check.why: All primaries are placed, so no data is missing (not red), but no replica can be placed on the same node as its primary.

check.q: You must ship logs from 200 small gateways with very little memory to Elasticsearch, with light JSON parsing on the way. Which shipper fits best?
options: Logstash on every gateway
Fluent Bit on every gateway
Kibana on every gateway
Elasticsearch on every gateway
check.why: Fluent Bit is a small C program built for exactly this, while Logstash runs on the JVM and needs far more memory.

interview.q: What is an inverted index, and why does it make Elasticsearch fast?
interview.a: An inverted index maps each token to the list of documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book. When a document is stored, Elasticsearch analyzes its text fields (splits them into words and usually lowercases them) and adds each token to that table. A search then looks up a few tokens and intersects their lists instead of scanning every document. The trade-off is that search matches tokens, so analyzers, mappings and phrase queries decide what you can find.

interview.q: What is the difference between ELK and EFK, and when would you choose Fluent Bit?
interview.a: Both use Elasticsearch to store and Kibana to search. ELK collects with Logstash, a JVM program that can do heavy transformations; EFK collects with Fluentd or Fluent Bit. I choose Fluent Bit when the shipper runs on many machines, such as every Kubernetes node. It is small (about 450 KB of memory against Fluentd's 60 MB or more) and can send straight to Elasticsearch. I would add Logstash or Fluentd as a central aggregator only if the pipeline needs transformations Fluent Bit cannot do.

interview.q: What should never go into logs, and how do you enforce it?
interview.a: Passwords, tokens, session IDs, connection strings, keys, payment card data and personal data such as emails should be removed, masked or hashed before the line is written. I enforce it in layers. The app's logging helpers mask known fields, code review checks new log statements, and a filter in the shipper is the last safety net. Scrubbing at the source matters most, because deleting a secret later from every index, replica and backup is hard.

deeper.body:
What happens when you run a search on `hello-logs-*`? The node that receives the request becomes the coordinator for that search, and it works in two rounds.

1. Query phase: the coordinator sends the query to one copy of every shard involved, primary or replica. Each shard searches its own inverted index on one thread and returns only the IDs and sort values of its best matches.
2. Fetch phase: the coordinator merges those short lists, picks the overall top results, and asks the right shards for the full documents.

This is why the shard count matters even on small data. A search over 30 daily indices with 1 shard each touches 30 shards. With 5 shards each it touches 150, and each one costs a thread and some memory. The Elastic sizing guide puts it plainly: searching a thousand 50 MB shards is much more expensive than searching one 50 GB shard with the same data. Most logging trouble with Elasticsearch at scale starts here, with too many small indices and shards (oversharding), for example one index per service per namespace per day.

Now the refresh. A new document first lands in an in-memory buffer. A refresh writes the buffer into a new segment, which is a small inverted index of its own, and opens it for search. By default Elasticsearch refreshes every second, but only on indices that received a search in the last 30 seconds. That is why the worked example added `?refresh=true` to its last write: it forced a refresh, so the very next search saw all three documents. For logs you never need that. A delay of a second is fine, and forcing refreshes on every write makes indexing slower.

The `_score` you saw in search results is relevance: how well a document matches the words you searched for. Product search lives on it. Logging mostly ignores it, because Kibana sorts log results by `@timestamp`, newest first.

One last check you can do right now: run `curl -s 'localhost:9200/_cat/segments/hello-logs-*?v'` while the lab takes traffic. Each line is a segment. Run it again later and the list may be shorter, because Lucene merges small segments into bigger ones in the background to keep searches cheap.

lessons.title: Running EFK on Kubernetes
lessons.goal: By the end you can run Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet with Helm, explain how a pod's log line gets its Kubernetes metadata, and give your log indices a mapping and a retention policy.

guess.q: Your kind cluster has 3 nodes and 12 pods. You install Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet that tolerates every node. How many Fluent Bit pods run?
options: 1, shared by the whole cluster
12, one next to each app pod
3, one on each node
As many as the autoscaler decides
guess.why: A DaemonSet runs one copy of its pod on every node it is allowed on, and that copy reads the log files of all pods on its node. Without the toleration in the lab's values, the control-plane node would be skipped and you would get 2.

terms.plain: A Kubernetes workload that runs one copy of a pod on every node, or on every node it is allowed on.
The folder on each node where every container's output appears as a file, one file per container.
The Fluent Bit filter that adds the pod name, namespace, labels and node to each log record.
Rules that glue the lines of one event, such as a stack trace, back into one record.
A rule that gives every new index whose name matches a pattern its settings and mappings.
One name for append-only, time-stamped data, backed by hidden indices that Elasticsearch rolls over for you.
Index lifecycle management: a policy that moves indices through phases such as hot and delete, by age or size.
How long you keep logs before they are deleted.

sections.h: One shipper per node: the DaemonSet
sections.body:
On Day 47 Docker handed each line to Fluent Bit. Kubernetes works differently. The container runtime on each node writes every container's stdout and stderr to a file, and the kubelet links those files into one folder:

`/var/log/containers/<pod>_<namespace>_<container>-<container id>.log`

So the job is "read every file in that folder on every node". A DaemonSet does exactly that. It runs one copy of a pod on each node, and the Fluent Bit chart mounts the node's `/var/log` into that pod. Add a node and Kubernetes starts another Fluent Bit there by itself.

Why not a log sidecar in every app pod? It works, but 40 app pods would mean 40 shippers instead of one per node, each with its own memory and config. Per-node agents are the common choice, and Fluent Bit's documentation says to deploy it as a DaemonSet.

Each line in those files is wrapped by the runtime. Here is one from the lab test, with the JSON shortened:

`2026-10-30T10:15:02.123456789Z stdout F {"level":"INFO","path":"/","status":200}`

That is a timestamp, the stream, a flag and the message. The flag is `F` for a full line, or `P` for a partial line, used when the runtime splits a very long line. The `tail` input with `multiline.parser: docker, cri` unwraps this format and joins `P` pieces back together. In the test, a line split into a `P` and an `F` part came out as one record.

Two more tail settings matter:
- `db` stores how far each file was read, so a restarted Fluent Bit continues where it stopped.
- On first start, Fluent Bit reads new lines only, so send fresh traffic before you go looking for logs.

sections.h: Who wrote this line? The Kubernetes filter
sections.body:
A bare log line does not say which pod wrote it. The `kubernetes` filter adds that. It gets the pod name, namespace and container name from the file name, for free. For labels and annotations it asks the Kubernetes API about the pod, then caches the answer so it does not ask again for every line. The chart creates a ServiceAccount and a ClusterRole that allow those reads.

Here is what Fluent Bit made of the line above in a test run, trimmed to the interesting fields:

`{"stream":"stdout","level":"INFO","path":"/","status":200,"kubernetes":{"pod_name":"hello-devops-7c9f8b6d5-x2x4k","namespace_name":"hello","labels":{"app":"hello-devops"},"host":"devops-worker","container_name":"web"}}`

Three settings in the lab's values shape that record:
- `merge_log: on` checks whether the line is JSON and, if so, lifts its keys (`level`, `path`, `status`) into real fields.
- `keep_log: off` drops the original JSON string after that, so you do not store everything twice.
- `k8s-logging.exclude: on` lets a pod opt out. Add the annotation `fluentbit.io/exclude: "true"` to a chatty pod and its lines are dropped at the node.

In Kibana these fields become filters you will use every day: `kubernetes.namespace_name: hello`, `kubernetes.labels.app: hello-devops`, or `kubernetes.host` to see whether one node is the problem.

The API lookups are the part that can hurt at scale. A thousand nodes asking the API server about pods adds real load. The filter has a `use_kubelet` option that asks the local kubelet instead. Your three-node kind cluster does not need it.

sections.h: Parsers and multiline logs
sections.body:
Parsing turns a string into fields. Fluent Bit has two kinds of parser, and you met both on Day 47:
- A parser reads one line, for example as JSON or with a regular expression, and turns it into fields. The lab's `json_line` parser does this for the access log.
- A multiline parser decides which lines belong together. Stack traces need this, because each line of a trace arrives as its own record.

Fluent Bit ships built-in multiline parsers for `docker`, `cri`, `go`, `java`, `json`, `python` and `ruby`. Treat them as a starting point and test them with your real logs. When I built the lab, the built-in `python` parser left Python 3.14 tracebacks in pieces. It expects each `File ...` line to be followed by exactly one code line, and newer Python versions add a third line of `^^^^` markers under the failing code.

So the lab defines its own rule, which is short:
1. A new event starts with `[` (gunicorn and Flask messages begin with a timestamp in brackets) or `{` (the JSON access log).
2. Any other line, including blank lines and `^^^^` lines, belongs to the event above it.

With that rule, one failed request became one 72-line document in Elasticsearch, with the traceback readable from top to bottom.

On Kubernetes there are two layers. `multiline.parser: docker, cri` on the tail input only joins lines the runtime split. Joining a stack trace is a second step, a `multiline` filter like the lab's. The best fix sits in the app: log errors as one JSON object with the stack trace inside one field, and nobody has to glue anything.

sections.h: Index templates, data streams and lifecycle
sections.body:
Day 47 left two problems: dynamic mapping guesses, and indices that never go away. Elasticsearch has a tool for each.

An index template is a rule: every new index whose name matches `hello-logs-*` gets these settings and this mapping. It only acts when an index is created, so today's index keeps its old settings until tomorrow's index appears.

Index lifecycle management (ILM) handles age. A policy lists phases, and an index moves through them:
- hot: the index takes new writes and most searches.
- warm and cold: older data on cheaper or slower nodes, searched less.
- delete: the index is removed.

Each phase has a `min_age`. The lab's policy has only hot and delete, with delete at 7 days. Daily indices make this easy to reason about: the index for 30 October is deleted about a week later, and ILM checks every 10 minutes by default.

Data streams are Elastic's recommended way to store logs. You write to one name, for example `logs-hello-default`. Behind it sit hidden backing indices such as `.ds-logs-hello-default-2026.10.30-000001`, and only the newest one takes writes. A rollover starts a new backing index when the current one is old or big enough. Every document must have an `@timestamp`, and documents are append-only.

I tested this with Fluent Bit. Any name that matches `logs-*-*` picks up Elasticsearch's built-in `logs` template, which in 9.x uses logsdb mode. Elastic's benchmarks found logsdb cut log storage by up to 60%. But the built-in `logs` policy only rolls over at 30 days or 50 GB. It has no delete phase, so data stays until you add retention yourself. The course lab keeps daily indices plus your own ILM policy, because every part of it is visible.

sections.h: What logs cost, and how to spend less
sections.body:
Logs are the signal that grows fastest, because every request writes at least one line. A simple way to think about the bill: what you store is roughly the daily volume, times one plus the number of replicas, times the days you keep it. Every one of those three is a lever.

Your lab already has a small example of waste. The hello-devops image has a Docker health check that calls `/healthz` every 30 seconds. That is 2,880 identical lines per container per day that nobody will read. On Kubernetes the kubelet's probes do the same, from the user agent `kube-probe`.

Ways to spend less, cheapest first:
1. Do not ship it. Drop noise at the node with a Fluent Bit `grep` filter, for example `exclude: path ^/healthz$`. Dropped lines cost nothing downstream.
2. Log less. Keep DEBUG off in production and avoid logging every loop iteration.
3. Keep it shorter. Seven days hot is plenty for many app logs. Audit logs may need a year, in a cheaper tier.
4. Copy it less. Low-value logs can live with zero replicas, if you accept losing them when a node dies.
5. Store it smaller. logsdb mode and good mappings, such as keyword instead of text where you never need full-text search, shrink indices.

Reliability is part of the cost too. If Elasticsearch is down, Fluent Bit buffers and retries. The lab's values retry without limit, so a short outage loses nothing. They also set `drop_unrecoverable_records: on`. A record Elasticsearch will never accept, such as one with a mapping conflict, is dropped instead of retried forever and blocking the queue behind it.

sections.h: Kibana dashboards and alerts
sections.body:
Discover is for reading. Dashboards are for the questions you ask every day. In Kibana you build visualizations with Lens, mostly by dragging fields, and pin them to a dashboard. A useful first logging dashboard for hello-devops has three panels:
- failed requests over time, split by `status`
- the top paths by number of 5xx responses
- a saved Discover session with the newest ERROR lines

Logs can also alert. Kibana's Elasticsearch query rule runs a query on a schedule, compares the number of matches to a threshold and runs actions when the condition is met. The query can be ES|QL, KQL or Elasticsearch's JSON query language. A rule such as "more than 3 documents with `status >= 500` in 5 minutes" is a few clicks. Actions go through connectors, and the Elastic docs note that some connector types are paid features.

Should alerts come from logs or from metrics? Prefer metrics for rates and latency: Prometheus from Part 9 is cheaper and faster for those. Use log alerts for events that only exist in logs. Good examples are a specific error message, a failed login burst or a payment provider's error code. One alert source per symptom keeps on-call sane.

sections.h: Loki or Elasticsearch?
sections.body:
Day 46 introduced Grafana Loki. It makes the opposite trade-off to Elasticsearch, so it is worth comparing them directly.

Elasticsearch indexes every word of every field. Any search, on any field, is fast, and so are aggregations such as "errors per path". You pay for that index in disk, memory and CPU.

Loki indexes only a small set of labels per log stream, such as `namespace` and `app`. The lines themselves are compressed into chunks in object storage such as S3. Loki's docs say this makes it less expensive to operate. The cost moves to query time: a search for a word inside the lines has to scan the chunks of every matching stream.

That leads to a different rule for each:
- In Loki, keep labels few and low in cardinality. Values such as user IDs or order IDs must not be labels, the same rule as Prometheus labels in Part 9.
- In Elasticsearch, put structure in fields, and watch the field count and the shard count.

How I would choose:
- Your team already runs Grafana and Prometheus, and most log questions start from "this service, this time window": start with Loki.
- You need fast free-text search across months of logs, heavy analytics on log fields, or security investigations: Elasticsearch or OpenSearch.

Many teams use both: Loki for everyday app logs, Elasticsearch for security and audit data. The shipper does not decide for you. Fluent Bit has outputs for both.

lessons.analogy: A DaemonSet of Fluent Bit is like a mail room on every floor of an office building. Each floor's mail room collects the letters its offices put out. It stamps each one with the sender's floor and department (the Kubernetes filter) and sends the sacks to one central archive (Elasticsearch). The archive's rules decide which shelf a letter goes on (the index template) and when old boxes go to the shredder (ILM). Where it breaks: a real mail room already knows who sits in which office. Fluent Bit has to ask the Kubernetes API for pod labels, and in a very large building those questions add up.

worked.title: Give hello-logs a mapping and a 7-day retention

steps.say: Start from the Day 47 lab with some logs in it. First the policy: indices stay hot, and are deleted once they are 7 days old. A policy does nothing until an index uses it.

Now the template. It matches every future `hello-logs-*` index and sets three things: one shard, zero replicas (one node, so a replica could never be placed), and the ILM policy. The mapping replaces Day 47's guesses: `path` becomes a keyword and `status` a small number.

Templates act only when an index is created, so today's index is still yellow with 1 replica. In this lab you can simply delete today's index (never do this to real data), and Fluent Bit creates a new one on its next write.
steps.code:
$ curl -s 'localhost:9200/_cat/indices/hello-logs-*?v&h=health,index,pri,rep,docs.count'
health index                 pri rep docs.count
yellow hello-logs-2026.10.30   1   1         79
$ curl -s -X DELETE localhost:9200/hello-logs-$(date -u +%Y.%m.%d)
{"acknowledged":true}

steps.say: Send a few requests and look again. The new index got its settings from the template: zero replicas, so the cluster is green.
steps.code:
$ for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s -o /dev/null localhost:8000/readyz; done; sleep 3
$ curl -s 'localhost:9200/_cat/indices/hello-logs-*?v&h=health,index,pri,rep,docs.count'
health index                 pri rep docs.count
green  hello-logs-2026.10.30   1   0          4

steps.say: Ask ILM what it thinks of the index. It is managed by `hello-logs-7d` and sits in the hot phase. It will move to delete once it is 7 days old.
Finally, check the mapping did its job. `path` is a keyword now, so filters and counts on it are exact, and `status` is a number. Tomorrow's index gets the same mapping without anyone touching it.

code.title: logging/fluent-bit-values.yaml
code.src:
# Values for the official Fluent Bit Helm chart (Day 48).
# Fluent Bit runs as a DaemonSet: one pod on every node of your kind cluster.
# Each pod reads the container log files on its node, adds Kubernetes
# metadata (namespace, pod, labels) and sends the records to the
# Elasticsearch from logging/compose.yaml, which runs outside the cluster.
#
# Install (check the chart's README for the current command):
#   helm repo add fluent https://fluent.github.io/helm-charts
#   helm upgrade --install fluent-bit fluent/fluent-bit \
#     --namespace logging --create-namespace -f logging/fluent-bit-values.yaml
#
# The chart ships its own default pipeline in the older "classic" format.
# We switch it off and hand Fluent Bit a YAML pipeline instead, in the same
# format as logging/fluent-bit.yaml.

kind: DaemonSet

# Run on the control-plane node too, so you also collect the logs of the
# Kubernetes system pods there. That node has a taint that keeps normal pods away.
tolerations:
  - key: node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane
    operator: Exists
    effect: NoSchedule

resources:
  requests:
    cpu: 50m
    memory: 64Mi
  limits:
    memory: 128Mi

# Read our YAML file instead of the chart's classic fluent-bit.conf.
args:
  - --workdir=/fluent-bit/etc
  - --config=/fluent-bit/etc/conf/fluent-bit.yaml

config:
  # Empty the classic sections so nobody mistakes them for the live config.
  service: ""
  inputs: ""
  filters: ""
  outputs: ""
  customParsers: ""

  extraFiles:
    fluent-bit.yaml: |
      service:
        flush: 1
        log_level: info
        # The chart's liveness and readiness probes call this HTTP server.
        http_server: on
        http_listen: 0.0.0.0
        http_port: 2020
        health_check: on

      pipeline:
        inputs:
          # Every container's stdout and stderr ends up in a file here,
          # named <pod>_<namespace>_<container>-<container id>.log
          - name: tail
            tag: kube.*
            path: /var/log/containers/*.log
            # The kubelet writes lines in the CRI format and splits very long
            # lines. These parsers unwrap the format and join the pieces.
            multiline.parser: docker, cri
            # Remember how far each file was read, so a restarted pod
            # continues where it stopped instead of sending everything again.
            db: /var/log/flb_kube.db
            mem_buf_limit: 5MB
            skip_long_lines: on

        filters:
          # Ask the Kubernetes API who wrote each line and add it to the record:
          # namespace, pod name, container name, labels, host (the node).
          - name: kubernetes
            match: 'kube.*'
            kube_url: https://kubernetes.default.svc:443
            kube_ca_file: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/ca.crt
            kube_token_file: /var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount/token
            kube_tag_prefix: kube.var.log.containers.
            merge_log: on      # if the line is JSON, lift its keys into fields
            keep_log: off      # and drop the raw JSON string after that
            labels: on
            annotations: off
            k8s-logging.exclude: on # a pod can opt out: fluentbit.io/exclude: "true"

        outputs:
          - name: es
            match: 'kube.*'
            # Docker Desktop (Mac and Windows) resolves host.docker.internal to
            # your laptop, where logging/compose.yaml publishes port 9200.
            # On Linux, use the gateway address from `docker network inspect kind`.
            host: host.docker.internal
            port: 9200
            logstash_format: on      # one index per day: k8s-logs-YYYY.MM.DD
            logstash_prefix: k8s-logs
            suppress_type_name: on   # required for Elasticsearch 8 and 9
            # Keep retrying while Elasticsearch is down or busy ...
            retry_limit: no_limits
            # ... but drop a record Elasticsearch will never accept (for
            # example a mapping conflict) instead of retrying it forever.

explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate how a line printed by a hello-devops pod gets into Elasticsearch with its pod name attached, and how old logs get deleted, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention the DaemonSet, the Kubernetes filter and ILM.
explain_back.answer: The container runtime writes the pod's output to a file under /var/log/containers on its node. The Fluent Bit pod that the DaemonSet runs on that node tails the file. The Kubernetes filter reads the pod name, namespace and container from the file name and asks the API server for the pod's labels, then adds them to the record. Fluent Bit sends the record to that day's k8s-logs index. An index template attaches an ILM policy to each new index, and ILM deletes the index once it is older than the retention we chose.

recap: Fluent Bit runs as a DaemonSet: one pod per node, tailing /var/log/containers.
The tail input's docker and cri parsers unwrap the runtime's line format and join split lines.
The Kubernetes filter adds pod, namespace, labels and node; merge_log lifts JSON keys into fields.
Index templates give new indices their mapping and settings; ILM deletes them when they are old.
Log cost is volume times copies times days: drop noise at the node first.
Loki indexes labels only and is cheaper; Elasticsearch indexes everything and searches anything.

check.q: You add a fourth node to your cluster. What happens to the Fluent Bit DaemonSet?
options: Nothing until you raise its replica count to 4
Kubernetes starts a Fluent Bit pod on the new node by itself
One existing Fluent Bit pod starts reading the new node's files too
You must reinstall the Helm chart so it sees the new node
check.why: A DaemonSet has no replica count; it keeps one pod on every node it is allowed on, including new ones.

check.q: You change the index template so new hello-logs indices have 0 replicas. Today's index is still yellow. Why?
options: Index templates only take effect after a restart of Elasticsearch
The template's priority is too low to win against the default
ILM has not reached the delete phase yet
Templates apply only when an index is created, and today's index already existed
check.why: Templates are read at index creation; existing indices keep their settings until you change them directly.

check.q: Your team often asks 'which requests mentioned order 8812 in the last 30 days?' across all services. Which store answers that fastest?
options: Elasticsearch, because every word in the log lines is indexed
Loki, because it stores lines in cheap object storage
Loki, after adding the order ID as a label on every stream
Prometheus, by adding order_id as a metric label
check.why: Free-text search over a long window is what a full inverted index is for. Order IDs as Loki or Prometheus labels would explode cardinality.

interview.q: How would you collect logs from all pods in a Kubernetes cluster?
interview.a: Apps write to stdout and stderr, and the runtime stores that in files under /var/log/containers on each node. I run a log agent such as Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet, so one pod per node tails those files with the docker and cri parsers. The Kubernetes filter adds namespace, pod, container and labels, and the output ships to a store such as Elasticsearch or Loki. I add an exclusion annotation for noisy pods, buffer and retry for outages, and alert when the agent itself reports errors.

interview.q: Our logging bill doubled. Where do you start?
interview.a: First I find where the volume comes from: the biggest indices, and the top services and messages by count. Most savings come from not shipping noise, such as health checks, debug logs and repeated lines, which I drop at the agent. Then I look at retention per log type, replica counts for low-value logs, and storage options such as logsdb or a cheaper tier for old data. I also agree on a rule with teams, such as a review for new high-volume log statements, so the bill does not drift back.

interview.q: When would you pick Loki over Elasticsearch?
interview.a: Loki indexes only labels and keeps compressed lines in object storage, so it is cheaper to run and fits teams that already use Grafana and Prometheus. It works best when queries start from a known service and time window. Elasticsearch indexes every word and field, which costs more but gives fast free-text search and analytics across long periods, useful for security and audit work. With high-cardinality values such as order IDs, Loki needs them in the log line, not in labels.

deeper.body:
You can point Fluent Bit at a data stream instead of daily indices, and it is a good way to see Elastic's defaults at work. I tested this trick against the lab. Keep `logstash_format: on`, so Fluent Bit still adds `@timestamp`, set `logstash_prefix: logs-hello` and `logstash_dateformat: default`. The date format is passed through as plain text, so every write goes to one name: `logs-hello-default`.

That name matches the `logs-*-*` pattern of Elasticsearch's built-in `logs` template, so the first write creates a data stream. Asking for it with `curl -s 'localhost:9200/_data_stream/logs-hello-default?pretty'` showed:
- backing index `.ds-logs-hello-default-2026.10.30-000001`
- template `logs`
- ILM policy `logs`
- index mode `logsdb`

The naming scheme is `type-dataset-namespace`. Here the type is `logs`, the dataset `hello`, and the namespace `default`. Elastic Agent and its integrations name their data streams the same way, which is why so many Kibana views look for `logs-*`.

Now read the policy behind it with `curl -s 'localhost:9200/_ilm/policy/logs?pretty'`. Its only phase is hot, with a rollover at 30 days or 50 GB per primary shard. There is no delete phase. A data stream on defaults keeps everything until the disk fills. To add retention, you can attach your own ILM policy with a delete phase. Or you can use the data stream lifecycle, a simpler mechanism that takes a single `data_retention` value such as `7d`. Read Elastic's data stream lifecycle page before you mix the two, because the data stream lifecycle leaves alone any backing index that ILM already manages. I saw exactly that in the test: setting `data_retention` on the stream was accepted, but the lifecycle explain API reported that the backing index was not managed by it.

Two practical differences from daily indices:
- You cannot delete "today's index" to pick up a new template, because writes always go to the stream. You trigger a rollover instead (`POST logs-hello-default/_rollover`), and the new backing index uses the current template.
- Data streams are append-only. If you ever need to update documents in place by `_id`, Elastic's docs point you back to aliases and plain indices.

For learning, daily indices show every moving part. For production on Elasticsearch 9, data streams with logsdb and an explicit retention are the default I would start from.

lessons.title: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
lessons.goal: By the end you can explain spans, traces and context propagation, run hello-devops under opentelemetry-instrument with a Collector and Jaeger, and use a trace to find the slow step of a request.

guess.q: One request to hello-devops took 835 ms. Its access log line says status 200, and the error rate on your dashboard is 0%. What shows you where those 835 ms went?
options: The gunicorn access log line for the request
The Prometheus counter hello_requests_total
The container's CPU graph for that minute
A trace of the request, split into timed spans
guess.why: Logs and metrics tell you that the request happened and how often. Only a trace records each step of one request with its own start time and duration, so you can see which step was slow.

terms.plain: The record of one request's whole path, made of spans that share one trace ID.
One timed operation inside a trace, such as handling GET / or sending one Redis command.
Passing the trace ID and the current span ID to the next service, usually in an HTTP header.
The W3C HTTP header that carries a version, the trace ID, the parent span ID and a sampled flag.
Keeping only some traces to save money. Head sampling decides at the start, tail sampling after the end.
The OpenTelemetry Protocol for sending telemetry: gRPC on port 4317, HTTP on port 4318.
A service that receives telemetry, processes it and exports it to one or more backends.
An open-source tracing backend that stores traces and shows them in a web UI.

sections.h: Why logs and metrics cannot find the slow step
sections.body:
Picture a checkout request on a payments site. It enters an API service, which calls a fraud check, which calls a card partner, while the API also writes to a database. The customer waited three seconds. Which hop took them?

Metrics give you averages per service: the 95th percentile of the fraud check went up. Logs give you lines per service, each with its own timestamp, and you have to guess which lines belong to this one request. Neither tells you that this request spent 2.6 of its 3 seconds waiting for the card partner.

A trace does. It is the story of one request, told as a tree of timed steps. Each step is a span: a name, a start time, an end time, and some facts about what happened. Draw the spans on a timeline, one row each, and the slow step is the longest bar with nothing underneath it. That picture is called a waterfall, and it is what Jaeger shows you.

Even hello-devops, one service and Redis, benefits. In the lab I paused Redis writes for 800 ms and sent one request. The trace showed `GET /` taking 835 ms, and its child span `INCRBY` taking 832 ms of them. Without the trace you see a slow request. With it you see a slow Redis call, and you know where to look next.

In Part 9 you met the signals, and here is how they divide the work in practice. A metric alert says something is wrong. A trace says where. The logs of that one request say why.

sections.h: Spans and traces
sections.body:
A span records one operation. In OpenTelemetry every span has:
- a name, such as `GET /` or `INCRBY`
- a start and end time, so a duration
- a trace ID, shared by every span in the same trace
- its own span ID, and the span ID of its parent
- attributes: key and value facts, such as `http.response.status_code = 200`
- events: timestamped notes inside the span, such as an exception
- a status: Unset, Ok or Error
- a kind: server, client, internal, producer or consumer

The parent span IDs make the tree. The first span of a request has no parent and is called the root span. In the lab, a normal request gives two spans with the same trace ID:
- `GET /`, kind server, 6.5 ms, from the Flask instrumentation. It is the root.
- `INCRBY`, kind client, 3.4 ms, from the Redis instrumentation. Its parent is the `GET /` span.

When Redis was stopped, both spans got status Error and an `exception` event with the type `redis.exceptions.ConnectionError`, its message and the stack trace. The trace carries the error with it, so you do not have to find the matching log line first.

Attribute names follow shared rules called semantic conventions, so every tool agrees that the HTTP method is `http.request.method`. Python instrumentation still uses older names unless you opt in with `OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN=http,database`, which the lab sets. Without it you see `http.method` and `net.peer.ip` instead. Tutorials use both, so do not be surprised by either.

sections.h: Context propagation and the traceparent header
sections.body:
Spans from different services only join into one trace if each service tells the next one which trace it is in. That hand-over is context propagation. The caller injects the context into the outgoing request, and the receiver extracts it and starts its own span as a child.

For HTTP, OpenTelemetry uses the W3C Trace Context header by default:

`traceparent: 00-4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736-00f067aa0ba902b7-01`

It has four parts, split by dashes:
1. `00` is the version of the format.
2. `4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736` is the trace ID: 32 hex characters (16 bytes).
3. `00f067aa0ba902b7` is the parent span ID: 16 hex characters, the caller's current span.
4. `01` is the flags. `01` means sampled: the caller is recording this trace.

You can play the caller yourself with curl, which is what the worked example does. Send that header to hello-devops, and Jaeger files the `GET /` span under trace `4bf92f...` with parent `00f067aa0ba902b7`. Jaeger also warns that this parent is not in the trace, which is true: curl never reported a span.

You rarely write this header by hand. Instrumented HTTP clients, such as Python's `requests` or the Java agent's HTTP clients, add it to every outgoing call. The trouble starts at hops that do not pass it on: a proxy that strips unknown headers, a message queue without instrumentation, or a homemade HTTP client. The trace then breaks into two traces that look unrelated. When a trace stops early in Jaeger, look for that hop first.

sections.h: OpenTelemetry: API, SDK, instrumentation
sections.body:
OpenTelemetry, OTel for short, is a CNCF project that standardizes how apps produce telemetry. It is not a backend: it stores nothing. It gives you these parts:
- the API: the functions your code calls to start spans
- the SDK: the engine behind the API, which samples, batches and exports
- instrumentation libraries, which create spans for frameworks such as Flask, Redis or JDBC
- OTLP, one protocol for traces, metrics and logs
- the Collector, covered in the next section

For many apps you write no tracing code. In Python, zero-code instrumentation takes three steps, and `tracing/Dockerfile.otel` does all three:
1. `pip install opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp`
2. `opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install` looks at your installed packages and adds the matching instrumentation. For hello-devops it found Flask, Redis and a dozen others.
3. Prefix your start command with `opentelemetry-instrument`. The lab runs `opentelemetry-instrument gunicorn ...` and `app.py` stays untouched.

Settings come from `OTEL_` environment variables, the same names in every language:
- `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME=hello-devops` names the service in every backend.
- `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT=http://otel-collector:4317` says where to send.
- `OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER=console` prints spans to the terminal, handy when no backend runs.

For your JVM services the idea is the same: add the OpenTelemetry Java agent with `-javaagent:opentelemetry-javaagent.jar`, set the same variables, and Spring, JDBC and HTTP clients get spans.

Auto-instrumentation shows the plumbing. For business steps, such as "price the basket", you add a manual span with the API, for example `with tracer.start_as_current_span("price-basket"):` in Python. One caveat from the OTel docs: gunicorn with several workers is fine for traces but breaks auto-instrumented metrics, which is why the lab switches metrics off.

sections.h: The Collector: receivers, processors, exporters
sections.body:
Apps can send spans straight to a backend. Most teams put an OpenTelemetry Collector in between, for three reasons:
- One place to change data: drop noise, remove personal data, add attributes.
- Apps stay simple: they send OTLP to one address and never learn about the backend.
- You can switch or add backends by editing one config file, without redeploying apps.

A Collector config has the same shape as Fluent Bit's pipeline from Day 47. Receivers take data in, processors change it, exporters send it out, and `service.pipelines` wires them together per signal. The lab's `tracing/otel-collector.yaml` reads like this:
1. The `otlp` receiver listens on 4317 (gRPC) and 4318 (HTTP).
2. `memory_limiter` refuses data before the Collector runs out of memory.
3. `transform/scrub` hashes `client.address`, because an IP address is personal data, and deletes `user_agent.original`.
4. The `otlp_grpc/jaeger` exporter sends batches to Jaeger, and `debug` prints a line per batch in the Collector's log.

In the lab, the hashed address really arrived in Jaeger as a 64-character hex string. The same caller always gets the same hash, so you can still count unique callers without storing who they are.

Version drift bites here. Collector v0.144 renamed the `otlp` exporter to `otlp_grpc` and `otlphttp` to `otlp_http`. The old names still work but log a deprecation warning. Older tutorials also show a `jaeger` exporter, which no longer exists. Jaeger speaks OTLP now. Even the core image's `attributes` processor warned that it leaves the core distribution in v0.167, which is why the lab uses `transform`.

There are two main Collector images. The core image, `otel/opentelemetry-collector`, is small and has the basics. The contrib image has the much larger set of components, including tail sampling.

sections.h: Sampling: head and tail
sections.body:
Tracing every request costs CPU in your app, network and storage. At high traffic most teams keep only some traces, which is sampling. The OpenTelemetry docs say that for high-volume systems a rate of 1% or lower often represents the rest very well.

The SDK's default sampler is `parentbased_always_on`. In plain words: follow the caller's decision if there is one, otherwise keep everything. That is right for a lab and usually wrong for a busy production service.

Head sampling decides when the trace starts, from the trace ID. Set `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER=parentbased_traceidratio` and `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG=0.1`, and about 1 trace in 10 is kept. I ran 200 requests that way against the lab and Jaeger held 17 of them. The decision then travels in the sampled flag of `traceparent`, so every service keeps or drops the same trace. You saw that in the lab too: a request with flag `00` left no trace at all.

Head sampling has a blind spot. It decides before anything has happened, so it cannot promise to keep the traces you care about most, the failed and the slow ones.

Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete. A Collector buffers the spans for a few seconds, looks at the whole trace, and applies rules such as:
- keep every trace with an error
- keep every trace slower than 500 ms
- keep 10% of everything else

The price is memory and a design rule: all spans of one trace must reach the same Collector instance. Tail sampling lives in the contrib Collector, and the deeper section shows a config.

sections.h: Backends, and joining traces to logs and metrics
sections.body:
The Collector sends spans somewhere that stores and shows them. The common open-source choices:
- Jaeger. Version 2 is built on the OpenTelemetry Collector itself, and version 1 has reached end of life. The all-in-one image you run in the lab keeps traces in memory, so they vanish on restart. For real use it stores to Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Cassandra or ClickHouse.
- Grafana Tempo, from Day 46. It needs only object storage and is queried with TraceQL.
- Commercial platforms. Dynatrace (Day 50) and Elastic both accept OTLP, so the same Collector config can send there.

Traces get most useful when the three signals point at each other. The thread that ties them together is the trace ID:
- In logs: write the trace ID on every line. For Python, `OTEL_PYTHON_LOGGING_AUTO_INSTRUMENTATION_ENABLED=true` adds it to log records. Then a Kibana search for one trace ID returns every log line of that request, across services.
- In metrics: Prometheus can attach a trace ID to a histogram sample, called an exemplar, so a latency spike on a Grafana graph links to an example trace.
- In the UI: Grafana and Kibana can link from a span to its logs and back.

A habit worth building: when you add a log line in a service that is traced, make sure the trace ID ends up in it. It costs a few bytes per line, and it is the difference between 'errors went up' and 'here is request 4bf92f..., and here is everything it did'.

lessons.analogy: A trace is a parcel's tracking history. The tracking number on the label (the trace ID in `traceparent`) is copied onto every new label as the parcel moves on. Each depot adds a scan with its arrival and departure times (a span). Looking at all the scans for one number shows where the parcel sat for two days. Where it breaks: a courier keeps every parcel's history. A busy system usually samples and keeps only some traces, so the request you care about may never have been recorded.

code.src:
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
# hello-devops with OpenTelemetry zero-code instrumentation (Day 49).
# Same app.py as the main Dockerfile, no code changes. opentelemetry-instrument
# starts gunicorn and patches Flask and the Redis client so they create spans.
#
# Build from the repository root (the folder with app.py):
#   docker build -f tracing/Dockerfile.otel -t hello-devops:otel .
# tracing/compose.yaml builds it for you.

FROM python:3.14-slim
WORKDIR /app
RUN python -m venv /venv
ENV PATH="/venv/bin:$PATH" PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1

# 1. The app's own dependencies.
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt

# 2. The OpenTelemetry SDK, the OTLP exporter and the opentelemetry-instrument command.
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir opentelemetry-distro opentelemetry-exporter-otlp

# 3. Look at the installed packages (Flask, Redis, ...) and install the
#    matching instrumentation packages.
RUN opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install

COPY app.py .

code.src:
# OpenTelemetry Collector for the tracing lab (Day 49).
# hello-devops sends spans here over OTLP. The Collector cleans them up and
# forwards them to Jaeger. Exporter names follow Collector v0.144 and later:
# otlp_grpc and otlp_http (older tutorials say otlp and otlphttp).

receivers:
  # Accept OTLP from apps: gRPC on 4317, HTTP on 4318.
  otlp:
    protocols:
      grpc:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4317
      http:
        endpoint: 0.0.0.0:4318

processors:
  # Refuse new data before the Collector runs out of memory.
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 200
    spike_limit_mib: 50

  # Change spans on their way through, with the OpenTelemetry Transformation
  # Language (OTTL). One statement per line, run in order.
  transform/scrub:
    error_mode: ignore
    trace_statements:
      # The caller's IP address is personal data. Keep a hash instead:
      # the same IP still gives the same value, but nobody can read it.
      - set(span.attributes["client.address"], SHA256(span.attributes["client.address"])) where span.attributes["client.address"] != nil
      # Nobody on the team needs the full browser string.
      - delete_key(span.attributes, "user_agent.original")

exporters:
  # Forward to Jaeger, which speaks OTLP too.
  otlp_grpc/jaeger:
    endpoint: jaeger:4317
    tls:
      insecure: true # plain text inside the compose network (lab only)
    sending_queue:
      batch: # send spans in batches, not one request per span

  # Print one line per batch in the Collector's own log, for debugging.
  debug:
    verbosity: basic

extensions:
  health_check:
    endpoint: 0.0.0.0:13133

service:
  extensions: [health_check]
  pipelines:
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, transform/scrub]
      exporters: [otlp_grpc/jaeger, debug]

code.src:
# Tracing lab (Day 49): hello-devops -> OpenTelemetry Collector -> Jaeger.
#
# Start (from this tracing/ folder):  docker compose up -d --build
# Jaeger UI:                          http://localhost:16686
# The app:                            http://localhost:8000
# Stop:                               docker compose down
#
# Jaeger keeps traces in memory only, so they are gone after a restart.

services:
  jaeger:
    image: jaegertracing/jaeger:2.22.0 # Jaeger v2, all-in-one (see README.md)
    ports:
      - "16686:16686" # the Jaeger UI

  otel-collector:
    image: otel/opentelemetry-collector:0.164.0
    command: ["--config=/etc/otelcol/config.yaml"]
    volumes:
      - ./otel-collector.yaml:/etc/otelcol/config.yaml:ro
    ports:
      - "4317:4317" # OTLP over gRPC, for apps on your laptop
      - "4318:4318" # OTLP over HTTP
    depends_on:
      - jaeger

  web:
    build:
      context: ..                         # the folder with app.py
      dockerfile: tracing/Dockerfile.otel # app.py unchanged, plus OpenTelemetry
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      APP_VERSION: "1.0.0"
      # OpenTelemetry settings. Every one is a standard OTEL_ variable.
      OTEL_SERVICE_NAME: hello-devops
      OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES: service.version=1.0.0,deployment.environment.name=lab
      OTEL_TRACES_EXPORTER: otlp
      # Gunicorn with several workers breaks OTel metrics (traces are fine), and
      # Prometheus already covers metrics in this course.
      OTEL_METRICS_EXPORTER: none
      OTEL_LOGS_EXPORTER: none
      OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT: http://otel-collector:4317
      OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_PROTOCOL: grpc
      # Use the stable attribute names (http.request.method, client.address, ...).
      OTEL_SEMCONV_STABILITY_OPT_IN: http,database
      # Keep every trace (the SDK default). Production systems usually sample.
      OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER: parentbased_always_on
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
      otel-collector:
        condition: service_started

  redis:
    image: redis:8-alpine
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5

A `jaeger:` exporter now stops the Collector with `'exporters' unknown type: "jaeger"`, and `otlp:` still works but logs `"otlp" alias is deprecated; use "otlp_grpc" instead`. lessons.real_world: A payments team traces every service with OpenTelemetry. Its Collector tier uses tail sampling to keep all traces with an error, all slower than two seconds, and 5% of the rest. The Collector also hashes client IPs and removes card-related attributes before anything leaves the cluster. When the checkout latency alert fires, on-call opens an example slow trace and sees the time spent in the call to the card partner. Then they search the logs by that trace ID.
