explain_back.prompt: Explain to a teammate how two services end up in the same trace in Jaeger, in 3 to 4 sentences. Mention spans, the traceparent header and the Collector.
explain_back.answer: Each service creates spans, timed records of its own work, and every span carries a trace ID plus the ID of its parent span. When service A calls service B, its instrumentation puts the trace ID and A's current span ID into the traceparent header. B reads that header and starts its own span as a child in the same trace. Both services send their spans over OTLP to the Collector, which can clean or sample them and then exports them to Jaeger, where they appear as one waterfall.

recap: A trace is one request's story: a tree of timed spans that share a trace ID.
The traceparent header carries the trace ID, the parent span ID and the sampled flag between services.
OpenTelemetry gives you the API, SDK, auto-instrumentation, OTLP and the Collector, but no storage.
opentelemetry-instrument traces a Python app with no code change, configured by OTEL_ variables.
The Collector's receivers, processors and exporters let you scrub, sample and route in one place.
Head sampling decides at the start; tail sampling in the Collector can keep every error and slow trace.

check.q: A trace in Jaeger shows the frontend span, but the payment service's spans for the same request appear as a separate trace. What is the most likely cause?
options: Jaeger's in-memory storage dropped half of the spans
The two services use different service names
The call between them did not carry the traceparent header
The payment service samples at 100% and the frontend at 10%
check.why: Without the propagated trace ID and parent span ID, the payment service starts a new trace of its own.

check.q: You must keep every trace that contains an error, but only about 5% of the successful ones. Where do you decide?
options: In each app's SDK, with a 5% ratio sampler
In a Collector with tail sampling, after the traces complete
In Jaeger, by deleting successful traces every night
In the traceparent header, by setting the flag to 05
check.why: Only a decision made after the trace ends can know whether it contained an error; the flag is just sampled or not.

check.q: You are about to add `user.email` as a span attribute so support can find a customer's requests. What does today's lab suggest instead?
options: Add it, because span attributes are internal debug data
Add it as the service name so it is easy to filter
Put it in the traceparent header so every service sees it
Hash or drop it in the Collector, or log a non-personal customer ID
check.why: Personal data in telemetry spreads to every backend; the lab's transform processor shows how to hash or delete it in one place.

interview.q: What is the difference between a trace and a span, and how does context propagation work?
interview.a: A span is one timed operation, such as an HTTP handler or a database call, with attributes, events and a status. A trace is all the spans of one request, linked by a shared trace ID and parent span IDs into a tree. When a service calls another, its instrumentation writes the trace ID and its current span ID into a header, by default the W3C traceparent header. The receiver reads it and makes its spans children of the caller's span, so both appear in one trace.

interview.q: Head sampling or tail sampling: what is the difference and when do you use each?
interview.a: Head sampling decides at the start of a trace, usually from the trace ID and a ratio, and the decision travels with the request so all services agree. It is cheap but blind: it may drop the rare error or slow trace. Tail sampling waits until a trace is complete, in a Collector, and can keep every error and slow trace plus a share of the rest. It needs memory for buffering, and all spans of a trace must reach the same Collector. So I use head sampling to cut volume, and tail sampling where error and latency traces matter.

interview.q: Why put an OpenTelemetry Collector between your apps and the tracing backend?
interview.a: Apps then only know one OTLP endpoint, so changing or adding a backend is a Collector config change instead of a redeploy of every app. The Collector is also the one place to process data: batching, retries, memory limits, removing personal data and tail sampling. It moves that work out of the app process. The cost is one more component to run and monitor, which is why small setups sometimes send straight to the backend.

deeper.body:
Tail sampling needs the contrib Collector (`otel/opentelemetry-collector-contrib`), because the `tail_sampling` processor is not in the core image. You add it to the processors of the traces pipeline, after `memory_limiter`. Its settings, from the processor's README:
- `decision_wait`: how long to buffer a trace's spans before deciding. The default is 30 seconds; 10 seconds is a common choice.
- `num_traces`: how many traces to hold in memory while waiting.
- `policies`: a list of rules. If any policy votes to sample, the trace is kept, unless a policy explicitly votes to drop it.

A policy list that matches the lesson looks like this, written in YAML under `policies`:
- `{name: errors, type: status_code, status_code: {status_codes: [ERROR]}}` keeps every trace with an error span.
- `{name: slow, type: latency, latency: {threshold_ms: 500}}` keeps every trace longer than 500 ms, measured from the earliest span start to the latest span end.
- `{name: some-of-the-rest, type: probabilistic, probabilistic: {sampling_percentage: 10}}` keeps 10% of everything else, chosen by hashing the trace ID.

Two consequences are worth thinking through before you run this in production.

First, memory. The Collector holds every span of every trace in flight for `decision_wait`. At 1,000 requests a second with 10 spans each, a 10-second wait means about 100,000 spans in memory at once. That is why `memory_limiter` comes first in the pipeline and why tail sampling Collectors get their own resource limits.

Second, scale-out. The README says all spans of a trace must be received by the same Collector instance. With three Collector replicas behind a normal load balancer, each one sees a third of every trace and decides badly. The usual fix is two tiers of Collectors. The first tier only forwards, with the load-balancing exporter, which routes spans by trace ID. The second tier does the tail sampling. The OpenTelemetry docs on scaling the Collector describe this layout.

Head and tail sampling can work together. A service can head-sample at 50% to cut the load on its own process, and the Collector then tail-samples what arrives. Just remember that anything head sampling dropped is gone for good, errors included. If you need every error, the SDK has to keep every trace, and only the Collector may sample.

For hello-devops there is a simple way to see the effect. Run the contrib image with these three policies, send 100 normal requests and 5 slow ones (with `CLIENT PAUSE`), and count traces in Jaeger. You should find all 5 slow ones and roughly 10 of the fast ones.

recap: Centralized logging copies every line to one searchable store, so logs outlive the containers that wrote them.
Write structured JSON logs with a level, and never log secrets or personal data.
Elasticsearch stores JSON documents in indices and finds them through an inverted index of whole tokens.
Mappings set field types: text is split into words, keyword is matched whole, and the first guess sticks.
A replica never shares a node with its primary, so a one-node cluster with replicas stays yellow.
On Kubernetes, Fluent Bit runs as a DaemonSet that tails /var/log/containers and adds pod metadata.
Index templates give new indices their mapping, and ILM deletes indices when they are old enough.
A trace is a tree of timed spans that share a trace ID, carried between services in the traceparent header.
OpenTelemetry instruments apps and the Collector scrubs, samples and routes their spans to a backend such as Jaeger.
Head sampling decides at the start of a trace; tail sampling in a Collector can keep every error and slow trace.

flashcards.front: Why can't you rely on `docker logs` or `kubectl logs` alone in production?
flashcards.back: The logs leave with the container or pod. Centralized logging keeps a copy that outlives them.
A table from each token to the documents that contain it, like the index at the back of a book.

flashcards.front: Why does a search for `payments` miss a log that says `Payment`?
flashcards.back: The default analyzer stored the token `payment`, and search matches whole tokens.

flashcards.front: text or keyword: which one for a `status` or `service` field you filter and count on?
flashcards.back: keyword. It stores the whole value, so exact filters and counts work.

flashcards.front: What does a yellow index mean?
flashcards.back: All primary shards are placed, but at least one replica is not.

flashcards.front: Which shard count is fixed when an index is created?
flashcards.back: The number of primary shards. Replicas can change at any time.
Elasticsearch, Fluentd or Fluent Bit, and Kibana.

flashcards.front: KQL to show only failed requests when `status` is a number field?
Why run Fluent Bit as a DaemonSet?
flashcards.back: It puts one shipper on every node, and each one tails the log files of the pods on its node.

flashcards.front: What does the Fluent Bit `merge_log` option do?
flashcards.back: If a log line is JSON, it lifts the keys into real fields of the record.

flashcards.front: When does an index template change affect an index?
flashcards.back: Only when a new matching index is created.

flashcards.front: Which ILM phase removes old indices?
flashcards.back: The delete phase, once the index is older than its `min_age`.

flashcards.front: The four parts of a traceparent header?
flashcards.back: Version, trace ID, parent span ID and flags (01 means sampled).

flashcards.front: What links a child span to its parent?
flashcards.back: The same trace ID, plus the parent's span ID stored in the child.

flashcards.front: How do you trace a Python app without changing its code?
flashcards.back: Install opentelemetry-distro, run opentelemetry-bootstrap -a install, and start it with opentelemetry-instrument.

flashcards.front: The three kinds of Collector components in a pipeline?
flashcards.back: Receivers take data in, processors change it, exporters send it out.

flashcards.front: What does tail sampling need that head sampling does not?
flashcards.back: All spans of a trace must reach one Collector, which buffers them until the trace is complete.

flashcards.front: What ties a log line to the trace of its request?
flashcards.back: The trace ID written into the log line.

quiz.q: A log message says `Payment FAILED for order 42`. With the default analyzer, which match query on the message finds it?
options: `fail`
`FAIL*` without wildcards enabled
`failed`
`ailed`
quiz.why: The analyzer stored the lowercase token `failed`, and a match query looks up whole tokens.

quiz.q: Your cluster turns red. What does that tell you?
options: At least one primary shard is not assigned, so some data cannot be searched
A replica is missing, but every document can still be searched
Disk use is above the high watermark on one of the nodes
Kibana has lost its connection to the cluster
quiz.why: Red means a primary shard is missing; yellow is the case where only replicas are missing.

quiz.q: A pod prints `{"level":"ERROR","path":"/pay"}`, but in Kibana you only see a `log` field holding that whole string. Which Fluent Bit setting is missing?
options: `keep_log: on` in the tail input
`merge_log: on` in the kubernetes filter
`suppress_type_name: on` in the output
`read_from_head: true` in the tail input
quiz.why: merge_log parses a JSON log line and lifts its keys into fields of the record.

quiz.q: Policy says app logs must be deleted 14 days after they are written. Your logs go to one index per day. What does the job?
options: Setting the index's number of replicas to 14
A Fluent Bit grep filter that drops lines older than 14 days
A Kibana alert rule that deletes old documents
An ILM policy with a delete phase at 14 days, set by a template
quiz.why: ILM moves each index through its phases by age, and the template attaches the policy to every new daily index.

quiz.q: A request arrives with `traceparent: 00-0af7651916cd43dd8448eb211c80319c-b7ad6b7169203331-00`. The service uses the default parent-based sampler. What happens?
options: The service starts a new trace with a fresh trace ID
The service records its spans, because the default is always on
The service does not record the request, following the caller's decision
The service rejects the request with an HTTP 400 error
quiz.why: The flags 00 mean not sampled, and a parent-based sampler follows the parent's decision.

quiz.q: You must remove the `enduser.id` attribute from every span before it leaves the cluster, for all services at once. Where is the best place?
options: A processor in the OpenTelemetry Collector's traces pipeline
A filter in the Jaeger UI that hides the attribute
An OTEL_ variable in each service that renames it
The receiver section of each service's Dockerfile
quiz.why: The Collector sees every span from every service, so one processor there scrubs them all.

quiz.q: You run three Collector replicas behind a normal round-robin load balancer and turn on tail sampling. What goes wrong?
options: Jaeger refuses spans that come from more than one Collector
Each replica sees only some spans of each trace
The traceparent header is lost between the replicas
Head sampling in the apps switches itself off
quiz.why: Tail sampling needs all spans of a trace in one Collector, which is why a load-balancing exporter routes by trace ID.

quiz.q: Two Python services run under opentelemetry-instrument, but Jaeger lists both as `unknown_service`. What did you forget?
options: Running opentelemetry-bootstrap a second time
Opening port 16686 in each service's container
Adding `@trace` annotations to every handler
Setting OTEL_SERVICE_NAME for each service
quiz.why: The service name comes from OTEL_SERVICE_NAME (or the service.name resource attribute), and without it the SDK uses a placeholder.

quiz.q: A container with Docker's default json-file logging driver crashes, and someone runs `docker rm` on it. What happens to its logs?
options: They stay in the image layers, so `docker logs` still works
Docker moves them to the next container started from the same image
They are deleted together with the container
They are sent to Docker Hub with the image
quiz.why: The json-file log belongs to the container and is removed with it, one more reason to ship logs somewhere central.

quiz.q: In Part 9 you kept Prometheus label values few. Which of these is the same mistake in Loki?
options: Using a label for the Kubernetes namespace
Putting each order ID in a stream label
Searching log lines for the word `timeout`
Keeping the log line as JSON text
quiz.why: Every new label value makes a new stream, so high-cardinality values such as order IDs belong in the line, not in labels.
